openItems.item: The disclosure heading is identical in both states ('What you can do in Claude with Smart Site'). In the setup state it describes what you get AFTER connecting rather than what you have now. Flagged as a copy decision the operator may want to revisit, not a defect.

fleetMemoryScratch.text: An ordering assertion written on bare indexOf passes when the thing it orders is ABSENT, because indexOf returns -1 and -1 is less than every real index. A positional test therefore needs a presence guard folded into the position lookup or it silently degrades into a check that cannot fail in the one case that matters. Proven here: violation A produced 'expected -1 to be greater than -1' from the guard, and without the guard that mutation would have gone green on the ordering test.

The discriminating violation for a placement requirement is PRESENT-BUT-WRONGLY-PLACED, not ABSENT. Removing the element fails both the presence and the ordering assertions, which proves nothing about whether the ordering assertion is independent. Moving it above the target failed ONLY the ordering test (1 failed | 30 passed), which is the proof. Any lane pinning a layout constraint should run the wrong-place mutation, not just the missing mutation.

cat -A in this Git Bash reported LF on a file that is actually CRLF; a Python repr read of the same bytes showed \r\n. A string replace built against the cat -A reading matched zero times. When scripting an edit against exact bytes on Windows, derive the line ending from the file inside the same instrument that does the replace, never from a shell tool's rendering of it. This is the enforcement rule about the instrument being part of the claim, in miniature.
